reviewStatus: Drafted from verified sources; pending independent clinician review before clinical release.
commonErrors: Assigning a degree on day one without follow-up.
name: Sunderland Classification of Nerve Injury

version.label: Sunderland (1951), first to fifth degree
version.detail: Mackinnon's sixth degree (mixed injury) is a later addition and is not included.

purpose: Grades peripheral nerve injury by the connective tissue layers disrupted.

options.label: First degree: Conduction block; axon intact (= neurapraxia)
Second degree: Axon disrupted; endoneurium intact (axonotmesis)
Third degree: Axon and endoneurium disrupted; perineurium intact
Fourth degree: Only epineurium intact (neuroma in continuity)

resultStates.label: Third degree
resultStates.summary: Axon and endoneurium disrupted; perineurium intact.

resultStates.label: Fourth degree
resultStates.detail: Little useful spontaneous recovery; surgical repair usually considered.

clinicalContext.text: Refines Seddon's axonotmesis into degrees with different recovery potential.

clinicalInsights.text: Fourth and fifth degree injuries do not recover usefully without repair.

limitations.text: The degree is usually inferred over time; not directly visible clinically.

limitations: Third and fourth degree injuries are hard to separate without surgical exploration.

confounders.effect: Different fascicles can have different degrees.

guideSections.howToPerform: Combine clinical recovery, serial neurophysiology and operative findings.
guideSections.clinicalContext: Guides decisions about exploration and repair.

sources.citation: Sunderland S. A classification of peripheral nerve injuries producing loss of function. Brain. 1951;74(4):491-516.
